title: Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents
pdf_path: papers/Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Not an adversarial attack paper: studies over-permissioning and agent mistakes; permission decisions are predicted from user/context/tool features, with confidence thresholds and human review. No attacker with cryptographic capabilities is modeled.
core_contributions: 205-person vignette study across 8 domains, 21 tools and 65 questions
Evidence that over-authorization is common and agent mistakes reduce willingness to authorize
Hybrid LLM in-context learning + LightGCN permission predictor
85.1% full-coverage accuracy on 7,563 decisions; 94.4% at 25.9% coverage
limitations: Only predicts permissions; does not enforce them
Cold-start accuracy 66.9%
Bottom-20% users only 69.7% accuracy
Does not model collaborative-filtering poisoning or group bias
Single-query vignette setting
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no formal security definitions or proofs
Permission prediction is a policy/ML problem, not a cryptographic authorization problem
applied_crypto_links: Mentions OAuth only as an example of install-time permission management (p.3)
TEE deployment listed as out of scope (p.5)
No credential, token, capability or enforcement mechanism implemented

title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
pdf_path: papers/SAGA_A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: Dolev-Yao network adversary plus malicious registered agents (C1-C5): protocol deviation, compromised agents, self-replication, credential sharing, Sybil. Provider and human authentication are trusted; cryptographic primitives and TLS are assumed secure. C3/C4 credential sharing and malicious Provider are not fully countered.
core_contributions: Provider-mediated agent registry and user-defined access contact policy
One-time-key based X25519 session establishment and access-control tokens
ProVerif symbolic verification of token secrecy and registration/communication authentication
Implementation and multi-region performance evaluation, plus RAFT replication and AWS scaling
limitations: No computational soundness proof; relies on symbolic ProVerif and standard primitive assumptions
Self-replicating agents and credential sharing (C3/C4) remain out of scope
Malicious Provider only mitigated by replication/audit, not formally modeled
Authorization policy is enforced by a trusted Provider; policy correctness is not cryptographic
Requires globally routable IPs; no NAT traversal
theoretical_crypto_links: Symbolic Dolev-Yao model and ProVerif proofs of authentication/secrecy
X25519 Diffie-Hellman, one-time keys, access-control tokens, X.509 identity
No new primitive or computational-security reduction (our inference)
applied_crypto_links: Provider-issued one-time keys and X25519 shared secrets
Access-control token encrypted under the shared key with nonce, expiry and quota
Mutual TLS for direct agent-to-agent requests

title: AirGapAgent: Protecting Privacy-Conscious Conversational Agents
threat_model_summary: Black-box third party knows the data schema, task, privacy instruction and agent design but not values or weights; it issues a single query that either preserves or hijacks the task context to extract contextually private fields. User, task and privacy instruction are trusted.
core_contributions: Context-hijacking attack that rewrites task context to loosen privacy norms
AirGapAgent: LLM data minimizer separated by a logical air gap from the third-party-facing model
20 synthetic profiles x 26 fields x 8 scenarios evaluation
Shows field-level minimization is imperfect and task specificity affects privacy/utility
limitations: Single-turn, text-only conversational setting; no tools, memory or planning
Logical isolation, not cryptographic or physical isolation
No formal privacy guarantee; LLM minimizer can over/under-select fields
Needs user escalation for fields outside U_min
Synthetic profiles may not represent real distributions
theoretical_crypto_links: None; contextual integrity is a normative privacy framework, not a cryptographic definition
Possible noninterference/quantitative-information-flow formalization is our inference only
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, OAuth, MPC, ZK or DP mechanism
The word 'encryption' appears only in an attacker-generated justification prompt (p.6)
DP is discussed only as related work
evidence_refs: pp.3-4 formal problem and threat model
p.12 Tables 6-7 field and task-specificity analysis

title: ISOLATEGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems
pdf_path: papers/IsolateGPT_An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: Malicious third-party apps and malicious content processed by benign apps; hub, operators and host OS are trusted, each app is untrusted, spokes do not trust each other. The system aims to block cross-app data theft, behavior manipulation and accidental exposure from natural-language ambiguity. Formal threat model absent.
core_contributions: Hub-and-spoke execution isolation architecture for multi-app LLM systems
Per-app spoke processes with dedicated LLM, memory and app
Inter-spoke communication protocol mediated by the hub with structured messages and permission prompts
Enhanced InjecAgent benchmark (1,598 attacks) and four case studies
Utility and performance evaluation against VANILLAGPT
limitations: Protection depends on users rejecting warned permission dialogs
No formal security definition or proof; OS-level isolation only
Single-app compromise is out of scope
Multi-app cold start and 10% tail latency overheads are significant
ISC lacks authentication for multi-host settings (our inference)
theoretical_crypto_links: Reference-monitor/noninterference formalization is our inference only
applied_crypto_links: Hub-assigned session IDs and structured ISC messages
Permission records and user approval UI

title: ACE: A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems
pdf_path: papers/ACE_A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: Weak and strong models: attacker controls one or more apps and their schema/description/outputs (strong model), can inject indirect prompts, but does not control the abstract planner, orchestrator or LLM. Query and context are trusted; app clearance labels are trusted configuration.
core_contributions: Three-stage architecture: abstract planner, concrete planner with lattice-based static IFC verification, isolated executor
Three new attacks on IsolateGPT: execution-flow interruption, execution-manager hijacking, planner manipulation
100% safety score on 1,054 INJECAGENT cases and near-zero attacker-app invocations on ASB
Utility evaluation on LangChain Tool Usage
limitations: No soundness guarantee because concrete plans are restricted to a Python subset
App clearance assignment/verification is not specified
Single-query, standalone-app scope
Trusted abstract planner/orchestrator/LLM and Docker isolation
Never calls a legitimate app with attacker-controlled output (design choice)
theoretical_crypto_links: Denning lattice IFC is a classical information-flow formalism, not a cryptographic definition
Possible formal noninterference proof is our inference
applied_crypto_links: No signatures, credentials, TEE, OAuth or encryption
